title: Dollar Investing for Nigerians: What Actually Happens to Your Money
excerpt: Follow the money from your naira account to a share in New York, and see where the costs really hide.
content:
Every week someone asks me the same question in a slightly different way. They have heard that Nigerians can buy Apple and Microsoft shares from their phone, and they want to know if it is real, or if it is one of those things that sounds good until your money disappears.

It is real. It is also more complicated than the adverts suggest. Not complicated in a way that should stop you, but complicated in ways that quietly eat your returns if nobody explains them. So let us follow the money, step by step, from your naira account to a share certificate in New York.

Step one: your naira has to become dollars

This is the step people skip when they calculate their returns, and it is usually the most expensive one.

You cannot buy a US share with naira. Somewhere in the chain, your naira is converted into dollars, and whoever performs that conversion takes a margin. Sometimes it is disclosed as a fee. More often it is hidden in the rate you are given, which will not be the rate you saw on the news.

Before you compare two platforms on their trading fees, compare them on their exchange rate. The trading fee might be a few hundred naira. The spread on the conversion can be several percent of everything you send. One of those numbers matters far more than the other.

Step two: you are now exposed to two things, not one

Here is the part that surprises people, usually pleasantly.

Once your money is in dollar assets, your return has two engines. The first is whether the shares went up. The second is what the naira did against the dollar while you were holding them.

If your shares rise 10 percent in dollar terms, and the naira weakens 20 percent against the dollar over the same period, your naira denominated gain is far larger than 10 percent. This is why dollar investing has felt so rewarding to Nigerians in recent years. A good chunk of the gain was not the companies performing. It was the currency moving.

Be honest with yourself about that, because it works in both directions. If the naira ever strengthens meaningfully, that same engine runs in reverse and eats into your returns. Currency is a tailwind until it is a headwind.

Step three: the platform matters more than the pick

Beginners spend most of their energy choosing which share to buy. Experienced investors spend most of their energy choosing who holds their money. The second question is the one that can cost you everything rather than merely cost you some upside.

Before you send money anywhere, get clear answers to these:

  • Who actually regulates this platform, and in which country? A licence somewhere unfamiliar is not the same as a licence somewhere accountable.
  • Are the shares held in your name, or pooled under the platform’s name? This determines what happens to your assets if the company fails.
  • Is there investor protection insurance, and what is the limit?
  • How do you get your money out, how long does it take, and what does that cost? Test this with a small amount before you trust it with a large one.

If a platform cannot answer those four questions clearly on its own website, that is your answer.

Step four: tax exists, quietly

The US withholds tax on dividends paid to foreign investors. The standard rate is 30 percent, and it is deducted before the money ever reaches you. Depending on the treaties in place and the paperwork your broker files, that number can sometimes be reduced.

Separately, you have obligations at home on foreign income. Most people investing small amounts never think about this, and then think about it very intensely at the worst possible moment. A short conversation with an accountant who understands cross border income is worth far more than it costs.

What I would tell a friend starting today

Start smaller than you want to. Your first transfer is not an investment, it is a test of the pipe. Send a modest amount, buy something, sell something, and withdraw it. Watch what arrives and how long it takes. You are buying information about whether this platform behaves the way it claims.

Then buy boring things. A broad index fund that owns hundreds of companies will not give you a story to tell at a party, but it will not depend on you being right about one company either. Most people who lose money in markets do not lose it by being too cautious.

And keep the currency effect in a separate column in your head. Know how much of your gain came from the businesses you own, and how much came from the naira moving. One of those you can reason about. The other you are simply along for the ride on.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
